newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST-Cifra Q1 net seen slightly weak.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Cifra Q1 net seen slightly weak.

text.p: Mexican retailer Cifra was expected to report weaker first quarter net earnings compared with a year ago, but analysts said the results would be more favorable on an operating basis.

A survey of four analysts predicted average net earnings of 400.54 million pesos for the first quarter (about 0.125 pesos per B share), down from 452.99 million pesos for the same period last year on an inflation-adjusted basis.
The culprit is likely to be weaker net interest earnings, a cash item below the operating line, analysts said.

"Net earnings will fall from last year, partly due to (lower) interest earned. In general we see the report coming in from average to good," said Silvia Espinosa, an analyst with the BBV-Probursa brokerage in Mexico City. Net interest earnings are seen falling due to lower interest rates in Mexico. Benchmark 28-day Cetes rates averaged 21.81 percent for the first quarter of 1997, down from 40.21 percent for the same period last year.

Operating earnings were seen growing slightly, however, to an average of 327.60 million pesos for the first quarter from 305.79 million for the same period of 1996. But revenues were not expected to grow in real terms due to weak consumer demand.

"The operating margin will be better due to the company's cost controls. I feel it was still a weak quarter for Cifra and the sector in general because we have not seen much increase in demand," said Christine Aimar, an analyst with Deutsche Morgan Greenfell in Mexico City.
First-quarter sales were forecast at an average of 6.311 billion pesos during the quarter, compared with 6.080 billion for the same quarter of 1996.
Analysts said Cifra sales would also be slow to recover as the company had a strong bias towards selling food rather than the general goods sold by rivals.

"We will see slower increases in sales when compared to other companies, as when the economy picks up people tend to buy more general goods such as clothing and domestic appliances," said Rolando Calderon, an analyst with Santander Investment in Mexico City.
